<!-- walkthrough: colonies -->
<!-- Monday: Countable Colonies -->

```{r cc-data, include=FALSE}
source("data/challenges/colonies.R")
```

##### Step 1: Look at the data

```{r cc-look}
colonies
typeof(colonies)
```

The counts are **text**, because of the `"TNTC"` plates (too numerous to count).

##### Step 2: Turn the counts into numbers

```{r cc-numeric}
counts <- as.numeric(colonies)   # "TNTC" becomes NA, with a warning
counts
```

##### Step 3: Keep only the countable plates

```{r cc-countable}
countable <- !is.na(counts) & counts >= 30 & counts <= 300
countable
sum(countable)
```

The plate with 16 colonies is too sparse to count reliably, so it's out.

##### Step 4: CFU per mL for each countable plate

CFU/mL = colonies ÷ (dilution × volume plated):

```{r cc-cfu}
cfu_per_ml <- counts[countable] / (dilution[countable] * volume_ml)
cfu_per_ml
```

##### Step 5: Mean, log10, round

```{r cc-answer-calc}
mean_cfu <- mean(cfu_per_ml)
mean_cfu
round(log10(mean_cfu), 2)
```

```{r cc-answer, include=FALSE}
answer <- sprintf("%.2f", round(log10(mean_cfu), 2))
```

**The answer is `r answer`**, i.e. about `r format(signif(mean_cfu, 2), scientific = TRUE)` CFU/mL.

##### The traps

Using every plate with a number, including the one with 16 colonies:

```{r cc-trap1}
all_plates <- !is.na(counts)
round(log10(mean(counts[all_plates] / (dilution[all_plates] * volume_ml))), 2)
```

Forgetting the plated volume (0.1 mL) gives a result 10 times too small:

```{r cc-trap2}
round(log10(mean(counts[countable] / dilution[countable])), 2)
```

**Lessons:** text in a numeric column turns everything into text; vectors of the same length line up element by element (each count with its own dilution); a logical vector selects the elements you want.


<!-- walkthrough: mice -->
<!-- Tuesday: Mouse Mismatch -->

##### Step 1: Read and look

Read both tables (the same files as in "Get the data") and look at them:

```{r mm-read}
weights   <- read.csv2("data/challenges/mouse_weights.csv")
genotypes <- read.csv("data/challenges/mouse_genotypes.csv")
head(weights)
head(genotypes)
```

The mice are in a **different order** in the two tables, so we can't just put the columns side by side.

##### Step 2: Check that the IDs match

Before merging, check that every ID appears in both tables:

```{r mm-ids}
weights$id %in% genotypes$id                   # is each weight ID in the genotype table?
weights$id[!weights$id %in% genotypes$id]      # which one isn't?
genotypes$id[!genotypes$id %in% weights$id]
```

`m07` was typed in lower case. Fix it with `toupper()`:

```{r mm-fix}
genotypes$id <- toupper(genotypes$id)
all(weights$id %in% genotypes$id)
```

##### Step 3: Merge by ID

```{r mm-merge}
mice <- merge(weights, genotypes, by = "id")
nrow(mice)          # all 20 mice
head(mice)
```

##### Step 4: Compare KO and WT

```{r mm-means}
mean_ko <- mean(mice$weight_g[mice$genotype == "KO"])
mean_wt <- mean(mice$weight_g[mice$genotype == "WT"])
mean_ko
mean_wt
round(mean_ko - mean_wt, 2)
```

```{r mm-answer, include=FALSE}
answer <- sprintf("%.2f", round(mean_ko - mean_wt, 2))
```

**The answer is `r answer`**: knockout mice are about `r answer` g heavier.

<details>
  <summary>The same with the tidyverse</summary>
```{r mm-tidy, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
genotypes |>
  mutate(id = toupper(id)) |>
  inner_join(weights, by = "id") |>
  group_by(genotype) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_weight = mean(weight_g))
```
</details>

##### The traps

Putting the columns side by side matches mice **by position**, so the genotypes end up attached to the wrong mice:

```{r mm-trap1}
wrong <- data.frame(weight_g = weights$weight_g, genotype = genotypes$genotype)
round(mean(wrong$weight_g[wrong$genotype == "KO"]) -
      mean(wrong$weight_g[wrong$genotype == "WT"]), 2)
```

Merging without fixing `m07` silently drops one mouse:

```{r mm-trap2}
mice19 <- merge(weights, read.csv("data/challenges/mouse_genotypes.csv"), by = "id")
nrow(mice19)
round(mean(mice19$weight_g[mice19$genotype == "KO"]) -
      mean(mice19$weight_g[mice19$genotype == "WT"]), 2)
```

**Lessons:** merge by ID, never by position. After a merge, check the number of rows.

**Coming on Wednesday:** is a difference of `r answer` g real, or could it be chance? The statistics lecture shows how to test it, e.g. with `t.test(weight_g ~ genotype, data = mice)`.

<!-- walkthrough: primers -->
<!-- Wednesday: Primer Pairs -->

##### Step 1: Read and inspect

```{r pp-read}
primers <- read.csv("data/challenges/primers.csv")   # the same file as in "Get the data"
str(primers)
table(primers$direction)
```

`table()` shows a problem: a few directions were typed as `r`, not `R`. Are the sequences all in upper case? Compare each one with its upper-case version:

```{r pp-messy}
primers$sequence[primers$sequence != toupper(primers$sequence)]
```

##### Step 2: Clean the data

```{r pp-clean}
primers$direction <- toupper(primers$direction)
primers$sequence  <- toupper(primers$sequence)
table(primers$direction)
```

##### Step 3: Write a function for one primer

Go through the sequence base by base with a `for` loop, and count the bases:

```{r pp-functions}
primer_stats <- function(seq) {
  n_gc <- 0
  n_at <- 0
  for (i in 1:nchar(seq)) {
    base <- substr(seq, i, i)
    if (base == "G" | base == "C") n_gc <- n_gc + 1
    if (base == "A" | base == "T") n_at <- n_at + 1
  }
  gc <- 100 * n_gc / nchar(seq)
  tm <- 2 * n_at + 4 * n_gc
  c(gc = gc, tm = tm)
}

primer_stats("GGCCAATT")   # test on a sequence where you know the answer: 50 % GC, Tm 24
```

##### Step 4: Use the function on every primer

A second loop goes through the rows:

```{r pp-apply}
primers$gc <- NA
primers$tm <- NA
for (i in 1:nrow(primers)) {
  stats <- primer_stats(primers$sequence[i])
  primers$gc[i] <- stats["gc"]
  primers$tm[i] <- stats["tm"]
}
head(primers)
```

##### Step 5: Put forward and reverse primers side by side

`merge()` by target. Columns from the forward primers get `.x`, columns from the reverse primers get `.y`:

```{r pp-pairs}
fwd <- primers[primers$direction == "F", ]
rev <- primers[primers$direction == "R", ]
pairs <- merge(fwd, rev, by = "target")
nrow(pairs)
```

##### Step 6: Apply the rules

```{r pp-rules}
pass <- pairs$gc.x >= 40 & pairs$gc.x <= 60 &
        pairs$gc.y >= 40 & pairs$gc.y <= 60 &
        pairs$tm.x >= 52 & pairs$tm.x <= 60 &
        pairs$tm.y >= 52 & pairs$tm.y <= 60 &
        abs(pairs$tm.x - pairs$tm.y) <= 2
sum(pass)

good <- pairs[pass, ]
good$mean_tm <- (good$tm.x + good$tm.y) / 2
good <- good[order(good$mean_tm, decreasing = TRUE), ]
good[, c("target", "tm.x", "tm.y", "mean_tm")]
```

```{r pp-answer, include=FALSE}
answer <- paste0(sum(pass), "-", good$target[1])
```

**The answer is `r answer`.**

<details>
  <summary>The same with the tidyverse</summary>
```{r pp-tidy, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
clean <- read.csv("data/challenges/primers.csv") |>
  mutate(direction = toupper(direction),
         sequence  = toupper(sequence))
clean$gc <- NA
clean$tm <- NA
for (i in 1:nrow(clean)) {
  stats <- primer_stats(clean$sequence[i])
  clean$gc[i] <- stats["gc"]
  clean$tm[i] <- stats["tm"]
}
inner_join(filter(clean, direction == "F"), filter(clean, direction == "R"),
           by = "target") |>
  filter(gc.x >= 40, gc.x <= 60, gc.y >= 40, gc.y <= 60,
         tm.x >= 52, tm.x <= 60, tm.y >= 52, tm.y <= 60,
         abs(tm.x - tm.y) <= 2) |>
  mutate(mean_tm = (tm.x + tm.y) / 2) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_tm)) |>
  select(target, tm.x, tm.y, mean_tm)
```
</details>

##### The traps

```{r pp-traps}
count_pass <- function(p) {
  for (i in 1:nrow(p)) {
    stats <- primer_stats(p$sequence[i])
    p$gc[i] <- stats["gc"]
    p$tm[i] <- stats["tm"]
  }
  m <- merge(p[p$direction == "F", ], p[p$direction == "R", ], by = "target")
  sum(m$gc.x >= 40 & m$gc.x <= 60 & m$gc.y >= 40 & m$gc.y <= 60 &
      m$tm.x >= 52 & m$tm.x <= 60 & m$tm.y >= 52 & m$tm.y <= 60 &
      abs(m$tm.x - m$tm.y) <= 2)
}
raw <- read.csv("data/challenges/primers.csv")
count_pass(raw)                                              # nothing cleaned
count_pass(transform(raw, sequence = toupper(sequence)))     # directions not fixed
count_pass(transform(raw, direction = toupper(direction)))   # sequences not fixed
```

Lower-case bases are not `"G"` or `"C"`, so they aren't counted. A reverse primer typed as `r` is missing when you select `direction == "R"`, so its pair disappears from the merge.

**Lessons:** look at your data (`table()` is great for spotting typos); write a function for one item, test it on input where you know the answer, then loop over all items.

<!-- walkthrough: imposter -->
<!-- Thursday: Who's the Imposter? -->

```{r im-packages, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
```

##### Step 1: Read and check

```{r im-read}
counts <- read.csv("data/challenges/counts.csv", row.names = 1)   # the same files as in "Get the data"
sheet  <- read.csv("data/challenges/sample_sheet.csv")
dim(counts)
head(sheet)
all(colnames(counts) %in% sheet$sample)   # do the sample names match?
```

##### Step 2: Normalise to counts per million (CPM)

Library sizes differ a lot, so raw counts can't be compared between samples:

```{r im-libsize}
colSums(counts)
cpm <- t(t(counts) / colSums(counts)) * 1e6
```

(Dividing a matrix by a vector works row by row, which is why we transpose, divide, and transpose back.)

##### Step 3: Pick out the sex-specific genes

```{r im-sexgenes}
y_genes <- c("RPS4Y1", "DDX3Y", "KDM5D", "UTY", "EIF1AY")
sex_expr <- data.frame(sample = colnames(cpm),
                       XIST   = cpm["XIST", ],
                       Y_mean = colMeans(cpm[y_genes, ]))
sex_expr <- merge(sex_expr, sheet, by = "sample")
sex_expr
```

##### Step 4: Plot

```{r im-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(sex_expr, aes(x = XIST, y = Y_mean, colour = sex, label = sample)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 15, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "XIST (CPM)", y = "Mean of 5 Y-chromosome genes (CPM)",
       colour = "Sex in\nsample sheet") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Female samples should be bottom right (high *XIST*, no Y genes), male samples top left. One sample labelled `F` sits with the males.

```{r im-find}
imposter <- sex_expr$sample[sex_expr$sex == "F" & sex_expr$Y_mean > sex_expr$XIST]
imposter
round(cpm["RPS4Y1", imposter])
```

```{r im-answer, include=FALSE}
answer <- paste0(imposter, "-", round(cpm["RPS4Y1", imposter]))
```

**The answer is `r answer`.**

##### The trap

Using raw counts instead of CPM gives the wrong number, and makes sample `S09` (a small library) look odd too:

```{r im-trap}
counts["RPS4Y1", imposter]
round(colSums(counts) / 1e6, 1)   # library sizes in millions
```

##### Bonus: the duplicate

Two samples are identical: a file was copied twice. A correlation of exactly 1 gives it away:

```{r im-bonus}
r <- cor(cpm)
round(r[c("S07", "S08", "S09", "S10", "S11", "S12"), c("S07", "S08", "S09", "S10", "S11", "S12")], 4)
```

`S08` and `S11` have a correlation of exactly 1: no two real samples are that similar. The base-graphics heatmap shows it too:

```{r im-heatmap, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
heatmap(r, symm = TRUE)
```

**Lessons:** normalise before comparing samples; check sample labels with biology you know (sex genes are the classic check); plot before you trust.
